title: Beatrix and the Autopsy
premise: When the coffin of town founder Edmund Voss is exhumed for an insurance fraud probe, it is found empty — and Hazel Galloway's photographic memory becomes both her greatest asset and her greatest danger. Following a trail of forged death certificates, she discovers that Voss faked his own burial with help from his daughter Beatrix, who has spent years quietly redistributing his fortune to families he ruined. As Hazel closes in on the truth, she must choose between handing Beatrix to the law and honoring the justice her father never received — and when the man who orchestrated the original fraud turns to murder to bury the past, Hazel realizes the empty coffin was never meant to stay empty. In the end, Hazel files a report declaring the remains unidentifiable, lets Beatrix vanish with the last of the money, and keeps one photograph — of the two of them together — as the only record that any of it happened.
about_author: R. M. Kavanagh is the pen name of a former claims adjuster from rural Vermont who spent eleven years reading other people's disasters in triplicate. Kavanagh writes mysteries about paperwork, small towns, and the lies people file neatly between the lines.

chapters.title: The Exhumation Order
chapters.summary: Hazel Galloway receives the court order authorizing the exhumation of Edmund Voss, dead five years, over a disputed life insurance payout. Her photographic memory flags something wrong in the file: the mortician's signature matches a document from a different case. POV Hazel. Beat: quiet unease beneath professional routine.

chapters.title: Dirt and Certainty
chapters.summary: At the cemetery, witnesses watch the coffin rise. Hazel memorizes every face in the crowd, including a veiled woman who leaves before the lid opens. The gravedigger mentions the soil was disturbed once before, years ago. POV Hazel. Beat: dread crystallizing into obsession.

chapters.title: Empty
chapters.summary: The coffin holds no body — only river stones wrapped in a funeral shroud. The coroner wants it ruled grave robbery; the insurance company wants fraud. Hazel alone notices the shroud was folded by someone who knew hospital linen protocol. POV Hazel. Beat: the case everyone closed reopens violently.

chapters.title: Beatrix
chapters.summary: Hazel interviews the deceased's daughter, Beatrix Voss, who runs the family foundation and grieves with suspicious composure. She answers every question perfectly — too perfectly, like someone rehearsing against a person with total recall. POV Hazel. Beat: fascination sharpening into suspicion, then something warmer.

chapters.title: Five Years of Alphabet
chapters.summary: Hazel returns to her archive of the town's insurance files and reconstructs Voss's final year: policies rewritten, beneficiaries changed, a fire at the mill nobody investigated. The pattern suggests Voss knew he was going to disappear. POV Hazel. Beat: the thrill of the hunt curdling as she implicates the dead man himself.

chapters.title: The Man Who Signed Twice
chapters.summary: Hazel tracks the mortician, Dale Pruitt, to a neighboring county and finds him drinking himself toward oblivion. He admits he signed papers he never should have — and that someone paid him in cash he never counted. Before he can name names, he bolts. POV Hazel. Beat: first proof of living conspirators.

chapters.title: What the River Keeps
chapters.summary: Following the stones' origin, Hazel searches the riverbank where Voss allegedly drowned and finds a rusted tackle box containing a second set of identification documents. Someone was watching the water long after the funeral. POV Hazel. Beat: the dead man becoming real to her.

chapters.title: Dinner with the Daughter
chapters.summary: Beatrix invites Hazel to the Voss house under the pretext of cooperation. Over dinner they circle each other with questions disguised as condolences. Hazel catches Beatrix watching her hands, cataloguing what she remembers. POV alternating close-third on both women. Beat: mutual recognition — two careful women seeing each other clearly.

chapters.title: Pruitt, Silenced
chapters.summary: Dale Pruitt is found dead in his motel room, staged as alcohol poisoning. Hazel photographs the scene and memorizes the details that don't fit: no bottle within reach, a receipt from a gas station forty miles away. The case now has a murderer. POV Hazel. Beat: grief and guilt — she got to him too late.

chapters.title: The Company Man
chapters.summary: Hazel's employer sends adjuster Marcus Webb to assist — or supervise. His questions are about Hazel, not the coffin, and his expense reports show he arrived days before the exhumation order. She begins keeping a second, private file. POV Hazel. Beat: paranoia; the institution itself may be compromised.

chapters.title: Ledgers of the Ruined
chapters.summary: Hazel traces the foundation's disbursements and finds anonymous payments matching, to the dollar, the losses of families Voss's mill destroyed decades ago. Someone has been executing a dead man's restitution. The handwriting on the authorization letters is Beatrix's. POV Hazel. Beat: the mystery reframes as moral — this is justice, not theft.

chapters.title: Edmund's Last Winter
chapters.summary: An elderly former nurse recalls treating Voss for terminal cancer in secret, and describes a daughter who refused to let her father be buried as a fraud while his victims went unpaid. The plan was his; the execution was hers. POV Hazel. Beat: sympathy overtakes suspicion; the law and the right thing split apart.

chapters.title: Webb Closes In
chapters.summary: Marcus Webb confronts Hazel with her unauthorized archive copies and offers a deal: hand over everything, implicate Beatrix, keep her job. He reveals the insurer's exposure is enormous and someone upstairs wants it buried — along with anyone who dug it up. POV Hazel. Beat: duty and survival pulling against conscience.

chapters.title: The Second Grave
chapters.summary: Acting on the nurse's hint, Hazel searches the old Voss orchard and finds a fresh-planted rose bed over disturbed earth. She doesn't dig. Instead she takes a single photograph and leaves it exactly as it is. POV Hazel. Beat: a deliberate act of mercy that makes her complicit.

chapters.title: Confession at the Foundation
chapters.summary: Beatrix finds the photograph on her desk and comes to Hazel at night, finally telling the whole truth: her father's body rests in the orchard, the stones were his instruction, and the money was his apology. She asks not for escape but for time to finish the last payments. POV Beatrix. Beat: love arriving precisely where duty forbids it.

chapters.title: Two Files
chapters.summary: Hazel builds two parallel cases: the official one pointing at a fictional grave robber, and the true one locked in her memory alone. Webb grows suspicious of her clean, too-tidy conclusions. Pruitt's killer is still out there, and the trail points toward Webb's own expense history. POV Hazel. Beat: tightrope tension; every choice costs something.

chapters.title: The Man Who Paid
chapters.summary: Hazel uncovers the original fraud: Voss's business partner, Aldous Crane, looted the mill, framed Voss for the losses, and has been the insurer's quiet consultant for years — the reason the exhumation was ordered, to destroy evidence Voss survived to testify. Crane killed Pruitt. POV Hazel. Beat: the villain revealed; the stakes turn lethal.

chapters.title: Night at the Orchard
chapters.summary: Crane, realizing Hazel knows, comes to the orchard to move the body and silence both women. Beatrix arrives to warn them; Hazel anticipated him, having tipped off the sheriff anonymously. A confrontation in the dark among the apple trees ends with Crane in custody — but only because Beatrix put herself between them. POV Hazel. Beat: climax; violence, courage, and the cost of choosing each other.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Crane confesses to Pruitt's murder and the original embezzlement, inadvertently confirming Voss died innocent. The exhumation scandal collapses into his crimes. But the empty coffin remains a felony, and the prosecutor needs someone to charge. POV Hazel. Beat: justice served for the past, jeopardy looming for Beatrix.

chapters.title: What Hazel Filed
chapters.summary: Hazel submits her final report: remains unrecoverable, probable historic grave desecration by unknown parties, case closed. She destroys her private file, keeping only one photograph. Webb accepts the report — and quietly returns the orchard photograph she 'lost,' saying some files shouldn't exist. POV Hazel. Beat: the lie told well enough to become mercy.

chapters.title: Departures
chapters.summary: Beatrix dissolves the foundation, its work complete, and prepares to leave town under a name her father chose for her years ago. At the bus depot she and Hazel say what neither will write down. Beatrix asks her to come; Hazel gives her the photograph instead. POV Beatrix. Beat: love acknowledged and released against duty's grain.

chapters.title: Alphabetized
chapters.summary: A year later, Hazel still keeps the town's secrets filed and alphabetized — except one folder, empty but never discarded, labeled with a name that isn't Beatrix's anymore. A postcard arrives with no signature, only a pressed apple blossom. Hazel smiles, files nothing, and keeps it. POV Hazel. Beat: resolution; memory as the truest inheritance, and hope left deliberately open.
